en: The Sūtra on the Parable of Salt Water, Spoken by the Buddha;
the translator’s name is lost, and it is now appended to the Catalogue of the Western Jin.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall speak to you, my disciples, on the seven matters concerning the parable of water. Listen attentively and reflect upon them well; I will now explain them."
They replied, “So be it,
World-Honored One! At that time,
the bhikṣus heard the instruction from the Buddha.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, bhikṣu?
What are the seven things compared to water?"
If a person is submerged in water;
or emerges from the water with their head above and then submerges again;
or emerges with their head above and surveys the four directions.
Some have emerged with their heads above water and do not submerge again;
some are about to emerge from the water;
and some are about to reach the other shore.
There are some who have already reached the further shore, having established their pure resolve upon that shore.
What kind of person is one who sinks in the water?

There is a certain person whose body is completely enveloped by unwholesome dharmas; being filled with pure demerit, he reaches hell for an eon, suffering punishment that cannot be cured. This is called a person who constantly sinks in the water; this is called the first instance of sinking when entering the water.
"What kind of person emerges from the water only to sink back down?

There is a certain person who, though immersed, possesses faith in wholesome dharmas, maintains a sense of shame and dread of blame, seeks the proper means, and feels shame and dread of blame regarding all wholesome dharmas; such a person emerges from the water only to sink back down. This is called the second type of person who sinks in the water."
"How does that person emerge from the water and look all around in the four directions?

There may be a person who, having emerged from the water, possesses faith in wholesome dharmas, possesses a sense of shame and dread of blame, and possesses a courageous mind, feeling shame and dread of blame regarding all unwholesome dharmas."
"He has emerged from the water and no longer sinks back into it.
Venerable friends, this is called the third person who is like one who has emerged from the water.
What kind of person is one who has emerged from the water and stands firm?"

Suppose there is a person who emerges from the water in this manner: they have faith in wholesome dharmas, possess a sense of shame and dread of blame, and are diligent; regarding all wholesome dharmas, they maintain a sense of shame and dread of blame. Such a person, having exhausted the three fetters, becomes a *srotāpanna* and does not fall back; they are destined to attain the goal and will certainly return to it. This is called the fourth person, who is like one emerging from the water and remaining there.
"How does that person emerge from the water and seek to reach the further shore? There may be a person who emerges from the water in this way:

he possesses faith in wholesome qualities, possesses a sense of shame and dread of blame, and possesses courageous intent; regarding all wholesome qualities, he is fully possessed of shame and dread of blame. Having exhausted the three fetters, with greed, hatred, and delusion attenuated, he becomes a *sakṛdāgāmin* (once-returner), who returns once more to this world to make an end of suffering. This is what is meant by that person being like one who emerges from the water and seeks to reach the further shore."
"How is it that those persons have reached the further shore? There is a certain person who emerges from the water;

they possess faith in wholesome qualities, possess a sense of shame and dread of wrongdoing, and possess courageous resolve. Regarding all wholesome qualities, they maintain a sense of shame and dread of wrongdoing. Such a person exhausts the five lower fetters, becomes a non-returner (*anāgāmin*), attains parinirvāṇa there, and does not return again to this world. This is called the sixth person, who, like one emerging from the water, has reached the further shore."
"How does that person have already reached the further shore and established their pure resolve upon the further shore?

There may be a person who emerges from the water, possessing faith in the wholesome dharmas, possessing a sense of shame and dread of blame, and possessing a courageous mind; they maintain a sense of shame and dread of blame toward all wholesome dharmas.

Or there may be a person who has exhausted all outflows (āsrava) and attained the outflow-free state, realizing liberation through mindfulness and liberation through wisdom, swiftly attaining direct realization in this present life, and dwelling in self-delight, having exhausted the source of birth and death."
The holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and one will no longer undergo rebirth in a mother’s womb.
This is called that person being like one who has already set foot in the water and has emerged onto the further shore.
"Thus it is, bhikṣus! Regarding these seven persons, I shall now speak to you and your fellow disciples using the metaphor of water.

This is what all the World-Honored Ones and their śrāvakas ought to teach: out of great compassion, desiring to bring about peace and security and to enable all to cross over, they prescribe dwelling in seclusion, at the foot of a tree, or in an open space under the stars. You should practice dhyāna and not be indolent."
"If you do not now apply yourselves with diligence, you will later have cause for regret.
This is what I command and exhort you.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Parable of Salt Water Spoken by the Buddha.
